Thank you for submitting your article "Automated cryo-EM structure refinement using correlation-driven molecular dynamics" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, including Axel Brunger as the Reviewing Editor, and the evaluation has been overseen by John Kuriyan as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: James S Fraser (Reviewer #2).

The Reviewing Editor and the reviewers believe that this paper would be of considerable general interest, provided that the validity of the method can be demonstrated in a convincing way. They continue to feel, however, that the demonstration that the method performs better than alternative methods is still not convincing. After discussion, we are prepared to consider a revised manuscript that addresses the concerns raised by reviewers. The eventual acceptance of this paper hinges on a satisfactory resolution of these issues. We recognize that the revisions would require a substantial amount of new work. If this is not possible, you might choose to submit this work elsewhere in its present form.

Summary:

In this revised manuscript, the authors have addressed many, but not all, of the concerns that were raised. The use of a "complete" empirical force field (rather than the simplified force fields commonly used in macromolecular refinement packages) seems to contribute to the differences when compared with other methods, along with the use of simulated annealing, and ramping up the resolution. While each of these individual approaches is not new, the authors suggest that the combination of them produces better quality EM structures. If this claim can be substantiated, it would represent a welcome new tool in the arsenal of refinement tools for EM structures. However, we are not convinced that the current manuscript definitely demonstrates such superiority, and major revisions are required for further consideration of this manuscript as outlined in the following.

Critical points to address:

1) Overall, while the manuscript has been improved by inclusion of multiple test-cases of different quality maps and comparisons to alternative (standard) methods. However, distinct alternative approaches were used for each test case and not applied across all examples. For example, MDFF was initially developed primarily for lower (~5-10 A) resolution cases, but is not used for the CorA example here (perhaps the strongest new result in the paper). Please consistently use a common set of alternative (standard) methods for all cases, and, additionally, use methods such as MDFF for the low resolution cases.

2) NSF test case, subsection “N-ethylmaleimide sensitive factor (NSF): comparison with Phenix”: for the re-refinement of the recent NSF/SNAP/SNARE EM single particle structure by White et al., 2018 (Figure 7 in the paper), the most significant advantage appears to be the substantially lower clash score compared to phenix refinement. The authors seem to be able to do better (especially for the clash score), without extensive grid searching (at least as far as we can tell). However, the clashscore itself does not indicate if their refined models are closer to the true structure. We had previously asked for the CABLAM analysis that should be included. Nevertheless, ultimately, the question arises if the re-refined structure is closer to the true structure of the 20S complex. Since there is no higher resolution structure of the entire complex available, the authors could test the quality of their refinement with the D2 domain of NSF by comparing it with the available high-resolution crystal structures.

Other important points to address:

1) NSF test case: "Finally we again point out the strong anti-correlation between the number of steric clashes and rotamer/Ramachandran outliers in the deposited reference and our models (discussed later in the Results section).” Which anti-correlation does this statement refer to?

2) Figure 7: the deposited 6MDO structure (referred to as the "reference" structure) actually has rather reasonable geometry. The improvement by the author's method is primarily a reduction of the clash score (Figure 7B). Please comment and speculate about the reasons (e.g., use of an accurate force field might clean up poorly determined regions?). Note that the Ramachandran statistics also slightly improves, contrary to the suggested anti-correlation (see previous point).

3) Figure 7A: Please calculate the heat map but compared to 6MDO instead of 3J94 as well since 6MDO and 3J94 are not equivalent models (e.g., they just pasted the SNAP-25 N terminal residues into 3J94, in which those residues do not exist in 3J94).

4) Figure 7A: it appears that their method mostly fixed the geometry of the solvent exposed parts of the model, so likely the ATP binding pocket is pretty much the same? These differences could possibly also arise from changes in rigid body positions of the domains in the hexamer. Please comment.

5) Figure 7: clarify how the various parameters for their refinement were chosen. Was there a lot of trial and error involved?

6) "Furthermore, the NSF refinement demonstrates the usefulness of the half-map-based cross-validation procedure as, for a refinement against a full map only, much more refinement runs have to done to identify the optimal map bias". Where is it is shown that more refinement runs have to be performed without access to half maps?

7) The question of whether a single model or an ensemble is more appropriate is worth discussing. For example, the three TRPV1 structures produced by independent refinement vary across the model (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and may suggest that an ensemble refinement may be suitable. Moreover, the discussion of "ideal geometry and over/underfitting" in the last paragraph of the subsection “Force-field dependence of the model geometry” completely ignores the effect of conformational heterogeneity that may be related to the non-ideal nature of refining a single conformation against an EM map. Ensemble averaging misinterpreted as a single structure is a possible reason. See Rice, Shamoo and Brünger, 1998, and Burnley et al., 2012 for crystallographic multi-start and ensemble refinements, respectively, and Herzik, Fraser and Lander et al., 2018 and Bonomi, Pellarin and Vendruscolo, et al.2018 for EM structure ensemble refinement. On the other hand, low determinacy of 3D classification and refinement of the particles may be another reason for the non-ideal nature of the refinement. These two issues are likely convoluted and represent a major challenge for the interpretation of single particle EM data. The authors are not expected to perform ensemble refinements, but rather, a discussion of this point is requested.

8) Note that the use of an empirical force field for crystallographic refinement was first suggested by Brunger et al., 1987, and re-investigated in more recent papers, e.g., Fenn et al., 2011. A discussion of this point would be appropriate.

9) How were the MolProbity statistics calculated? There are some subtleties that might need to be taken into consideration. By default Molprobity uses bond lengths for hydrogen atoms that are centered on the X-ray scattering position (electron cloud), as opposed to the nuclear position of the atom – i.e. the former is shorter than the latter (see Protein Sci. 2018, 27:293-315). This can have some consequences depending on the workflow. If MolProbity is given a model containing hydrogen atoms whose positions have been defined using nuclear positions the clash score may be reported as high. Alternatively, if a model is optimized using nuclear position hydrogen atoms, and these are removed, MolProbity automatically adds hydrogen atoms at the electron cloud position, resulting in systematically low clash scores. The authors should consider their protocol in light of this, and make it clear what was done in the Materials and methods section.

10) Is a complete model a requirement for the method? In the Materials and methods section it appears that any missing residues in the test structures were "filled in" using homology modeling or other approaches. Is this mandatory? If so it needs to be clearly communicated in the paper. The creation of parts of models for which there is no clear experimental data to support that model are questionable.

11) The authors make an interesting argument about clashes and side- and mainchain outliers. However, arguing that a very low clash score and a significant number of geometry outliers is reasonable stretches credulity. It is well known from high resolution structures what the expectations are for outliers. It is also observed that at lower resolution it becomes increasingly hard to determine correct rotamer and mainchain conformations based on the experimental data. The authors might be better off to emphasize that they are able to create models with a quality consistent with many other methods at this resolution, often better than the starting models, and accept that there is room for improvement.

12) The authors should be clear what they mean when they use the phrase "overfitting" in this context. There is often confusion about this term's meaning – e.g. fitting of noise, model correctness, determination of the optimal protocol.

13) It would seem appropriate to mention the work of Sanbonmatsu and colleagues: Kirmizialtin et al., 2015.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Automated cryo-EM structure refinement using correlation-driven molecular dynamics" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by John Kuriyan (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor, and three reviewers.

We thank you for addressing many of our concerns, in particular with the new discussion sections, the CorA analysis, and the comparisons for all refinements. The application to NSF shows that the method can obtain a model that is closer to the true structure as assessed by the agreement with the high-resolution crystal structures of the NSF D2 domain. In particular, the improved placement of the nucleotide is impressive. However, there are some remaining minor issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

1. Please provide the CABLAM and other statistics (provided in the supplemental files as. tex files) as proper tables.

2. You are correct in their assertion that the CDMD procedure has a larger radius of convergence than the Refmac, Phenix and Rosetta procedures. However, while it is very much appreciated that making use of other programs can be challenging, it is probable that some of the protocols used are not optimal for the particular cases being studied. For example, in the case of phenix.real_space_refine the default protocols are appropriate for refinement of models close to correct, i.e. not significantly displaced from the cryo-EM volume (globally or locally). Moreover, the protocol outlined in White et al., 2018 helps extend the radius of convergence. However, for models that have more significant starting errors, morphing is an important option for increasing the radius of convergence. It can also be necessary to run more refinement cycles to increase the convergence radius. Please comment in the Discussion.

3. The benchmark information in Table 2 is likely to be confusing for many readers (the timings provided in the Benchmark text are very useful). Would it be possible to provide statistics in the form of total run times for refinements in a table form?

results.result: CDMD is a novel automated method for refining atomistic models into cryo-EM maps across a wide resolution range (near-atomic to subnanometer). The method combines a chemically accurate force field with thermodynamic sampling, employs gradual resolution increase and simulated annealing, and requires no manual intervention or additional restraints. It has been implemented in the GPU-accelerated GROMACS MD suite with only three control parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C22, C175-C176 collectively establish the core methodology of CDMD. The abstract and introduction provide clear descriptions of the method's capabilities, technical approach, and implementation. The method is well-defined with specific technical details about the force field, sampling strategy, and automation features.

results.result: CDMD was validated on diverse test cases at resolutions of 2.6-7 Å and demonstrated superior performance compared to established methods (Phenix, Rosetta, Refmac) in most cases. The method has a radius of convergence of at least 6-7 Å (overall RMSD) and 25 Å (local deviations), which is comparable to recent MDFF versions and superior to non-MD methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C23-C24, C160-C162 are supported by extensive comparative testing across multiple systems (aldolase, tubulin, TRPV1, NSF, nucleosome, ribosome, CorA). The manuscript provides detailed quantitative comparisons with alternative methods and demonstrates CDMD's advantages in convergence and accuracy across different resolution ranges.

results.result: For the aldolase system (2.6 Å resolution), CDMD successfully refined a starting model with RMSD ≈6.6 Å to achieve RMSDref ≈1.8 Å from the reference structure. The refinement maintained good geometry throughout and showed no overfitting based on half-map cross-validation. Only Rosetta achieved comparable convergence among alternative methods, while Phenix and Refmac showed poorer performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C51 describe the aldolase refinement results with specific quantitative metrics (RMSD values, force constants, FSC analysis). The half-map validation protocol (C39, C43) provides evidence against overfitting. Comparisons with control X-ray structures (C38, C50) and alternative methods (C47-C49) support the conclusions about CDMD's performance.

results.result: For the tubulin system (4.1 Å medium-resolution map), CDMD refined a curved GDP-tubulin structure to the straight microtubule-like conformation, achieving reciprocal-space correlation comparable to high-resolution control structures (3.3-3.5 Å). The method demonstrated ability to provide plausible local geometries when information is not fully present in the map, with only Phenix producing comparable results among alternative methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C62 are supported by detailed FSC analysis (C55), cross-validation (C56), stereochemical quality assessment (C57-C58), and comparisons with control structures and alternative methods (C59-C61). The results demonstrate CDMD's capability at medium resolutions where the force field must compensate for incomplete density information.

results.result: For the TRPV1 system (3.2 Å with local resolution 2.5-7 Å), CDMD successfully refined a distant starting model (RMSDref ≈5 Å with local deviations up to ≈20 Å) to achieve RMSDref ≈2.5 Å with good geometry. The method handled highly heterogeneous local resolution, with three independent refinements producing consistent structures in high-resolution regions and expected variability in low-resolution regions. Alternative methods failed to achieve comparable convergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C74 demonstrate CDMD's robustness to heterogeneous resolution and large initial deviations. The reproducibility analysis (C73) and comparison with alternative methods (C70-C72) support the conclusions. The results show CDMD's ability to handle challenging cases where local resolution varies dramatically across the structure.

results.result: In comparisons with previously published Rosetta and ReMDFF models for TRPV1, CDMD produced models with comparable or superior quality. The CDMD model outperformed ReMDFF in both reciprocal-space correlation and model geometry, particularly in the low-resolution ARD region, despite ReMDFF also using an atomistic force field.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C82 provide direct comparisons with published models from other MD-based methods. The quantitative comparisons (FSC, geometry statistics) support the superiority of CDMD over ReMDFF (C80-C82). The comparison is fair as both methods use atomistic force fields, highlighting the advantage of CDMD's correlation-based potential.

results.result: For the NSF system (3.9 Å), CDMD was compared with the newest Phenix protocol using optimized parameters. Without half-maps for validation, multiple refinements at different force constants (2-8 × 10^5 kJ/mol) were performed. The CDMD model showed substantially lower clashscore and systematically lower RMSD to control structures (≈0.2 Å difference) compared to the deposited Phenix model, with better ATP binding pocket geometry. Alternative methods showed only ≈0.5 Å improvement versus ≈2 Å for CDMD.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C101 describe a rigorous comparison with state-of-the-art Phenix refinement. The systematic testing of force constants (C88, C90) addresses the lack of half-maps. Comparisons with high-resolution X-ray controls (C87, C95-C96) validate the superior accuracy of CDMD. The results demonstrate CDMD's advantages even when compared to optimized protocols from established methods.

results.result: For the nucleosome system (3.7 Å), CDMD refined a 'breathing' nucleosome structure into the canonical state, involving non-rigid-body transitions including DNA shift by ≈1 base pair. The CDMD model achieved high DNA quality (RMSD ≈1.4 Å to controls) without geometry restraints, despite using the CHARMM force field which is inaccurate for DNA in plain MD simulations. Only CDMD achieved model accuracy comparable to the deposited reference among tested methods, with alternative methods showing poor DNA refinement.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C119 demonstrate CDMD's capability for complex protein-DNA systems undergoing non-trivial conformational changes. The DNA quality achievement (C111, C113) is particularly remarkable given the force field limitations, supporting the importance of the 'soft' fitting potential (C114). Comparisons with alternative methods (C115-C119) show clear advantages for CDMD in handling mixed protein-DNA systems.

results.result: For the 70S ribosome system, a distant starting model in the codon reading state (PDB ID: 5LZC) was prepared and refined into the GTPase-activated state map (3.4 Å). The system was prepared using AMBERFF12sb force field with appropriate ion placement and solvation.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C174 describe the ribosome system preparation with appropriate citations. The methods are clearly documented and follow established protocols for large RNA-protein complexes. This represents proper experimental design for testing CDMD on a very large and complex system.

results.result: For the CorA magnesium transporter (7.1 Å low-resolution map), CDMD refined the closed symmetric structure into an asymmetric open state with RMSD ≈25 Å in some regions. The CDMD model showed gate opening with increased pore volume and solvation, consistent with biochemical and simulation data. In contrast, MDFF (with or without restraints) failed to induce gate opening, attributed to the 'hard' MDFF potential restricting the model to highest-density regions, while CDMD's 'soft' correlation-based potential allows more internal flexibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C139 demonstrate CDMD's capability for low-resolution refinement involving large conformational changes. The comparison with MDFF (C125-C138) is particularly informative, showing that CDMD's correlation-based potential enables biologically relevant transitions that MDFF cannot achieve. The agreement with prior biochemical data (C134) provides external validation, though the authors appropriately note that higher-resolution controls are still needed for full validation.

results.result: Analysis of rotamer and Ramachandran outliers in CDMD models revealed that structural errors are likely a combination of cryo-EM data-specific outliers and force field artifacts. CDMD refinement reduces overall outlier occurrence, but certain residue types (aspartates, leucines, tryptophans, valines for CHARMM; threonines and valines for AMBER) show systematic force-field-specific errors. The reduction in steric clashes by CDMD often comes at the cost of increased rotamer/Ramachandran outliers compared to deposited models.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C148 provide a thorough per-residue analysis of structural errors with appropriate statistical support. The analysis distinguishes between force-field-specific systematic errors (C145-C147) and data-driven improvements (C143-C144), supporting the conclusion of combined effects (C148). This represents an honest assessment of method limitations and their sources.

results.result: The quality of refined structures is limited by the experimental map quality, with potential issues from 3D classification, particle alignment, and conformational heterogeneity. The study focused on single-structure refinement, which is appropriate for high-resolution maps but may not be optimal for medium/low-resolution maps where ensemble refinement might be needed. Despite force field limitations, CDMD generates models with quality consistent with established methods given the map quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C159 provide appropriate caveats and context for interpreting the results. The discussion of ensemble refinement (C151, C154-C155) acknowledges limitations of single-structure approaches. The acknowledgment of force field development challenges (C156-C158) is honest and appropriate. The conclusion (C159) is appropriately qualified given the identified limitations.

results.result: CDMD addresses the challenge of reconciling local refinement accuracy with large convergence radius through proper treatment of concerted molecular motions. The method overcomes shortcomings of existing methods (poor convergence/accuracy of non-MD methods at medium/low resolution; poor performance of MD-based methods at high resolution) by integrating established techniques (correlation potential, simulated annealing) with chemically accurate force fields, adaptive resolution, and half-map validation.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C164, C166-C167 summarize the key advantages of CDMD based on the extensive validation across multiple systems. The conclusions are well-supported by the comparative results showing CDMD's superior performance across different resolution ranges and system types. The integration of multiple techniques into an optimized protocol represents a significant methodological advance.

results.result: CDMD employs several technical innovations: only the simulated density is resampled (not the experimental density), higher force constants are used at late stages for high-resolution maps to ensure accurate side chain fitting, and high-temperature simulated annealing enhances local map-model agreement while preserving well-refined regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C34-C35 describe specific technical features of the CDMD protocol with appropriate citations to distinguish from previous approaches. These features are well-justified based on the physical considerations (thermal fluctuations, sampling efficiency) and are demonstrated to work effectively in the test cases.

results.result: CDMD is flexible and can be used for quick re-refinement of close starting models against high-resolution maps or flexible fitting of distant models into low-resolution maps. The GPU-accelerated GROMACS implementation provides good trade-off between refinement time and hardware cost. Combined with de novo building tools, CDMD provides a fully automated framework for cryo-EM data interpretation.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C170 describe the practical utility and implementation of CDMD. The flexibility claim (C168) is supported by the diverse test cases. The computational efficiency claim (C169) is supported by benchmark data in the methods section. The automation claim (C170) is supported by the demonstrated protocol requiring no manual intervention.

results.result: Different force fields were used for different systems: CHARMM36m for CorA (for consistency with MDFF comparison), CHARMM22* for other non-ribosomal systems, and AMBERFF12sb for the ribosome.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C178 document the force field choices with appropriate citations. The choice of CHARMM36m for CorA to enable fair comparison with MDFF is methodologically sound. The documentation of force field choices is important for reproducibility and interpretation of results.

results.result: The introduction establishes the context for CDMD by reviewing the state of cryo-EM and existing refinement methods. Cryo-EM has achieved near-atomic resolution, but methods for deriving accurate atomistic models lag behind. Existing non-MD methods have limitations at medium/low resolution (clashes, poor geometry), while MD-based methods face challenges at high resolution (trapping, force field dependencies). No existing method simultaneously achieves resolution-independent fitting, stereochemical accuracy, and automation.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C21 provide appropriate background with extensive citations to support each statement about the field. The characterization of existing methods' limitations is fair and well-documented. The identification of the gap that CDMD addresses (C21) is well-justified based on the cited literature.
